topics.title: Water scarcity and the need for conservation

learn.hook: Water is renewable — the water cycle keeps refilling it — so why do so many Indian towns queue up for tankers every summer?
points: Fresh water is renewed by the hydrological (water) cycle, yet many regions face water scarcity.
Scarcity is often caused not by low rainfall alone but by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups.
A growing population needs more food, so more land is irrigated, even in the dry season; heavy pumping of groundwater through wells and tube wells lowers the water table.
Industries need water and also power, much of which comes from hydroelectricity. Growing cities make things worse — many housing societies pump their own groundwater.
Even where there is plenty of water, it may be unfit to use because of domestic and industrial waste, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers — this also causes scarcity.

example.q: A city gets good rainfall, yet many families buy drinking water. Give two possible reasons.
steps: Check quantity: is there enough water? Rainfall is good, so quantity may not be the problem.
Check quality: sewage or factory waste may have polluted the local river or lake.
Check access: groundwater may be over-pumped or unequally shared, so some areas get too little.
example.answer: Water pollution and over-use or unequal access can cause scarcity even where rainfall is good.

learn.reallife: Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth and reusing RO waste water to mop the floor are small ways your family can fight water scarcity.

games.title: Water scarcity: true or false?
items: Water scarcity can occur even in areas with good rainfall.
Pollution, over-use and unequal access can cause scarcity anywhere.
Over-pumping of groundwater lowers the water table.
When water is pumped out faster than it is refilled, the water table falls.
Polluted water does not cause water scarcity because the amount of water stays the same.
Water that is unfit to use does not meet our needs, so it causes scarcity.
Growing cities increase the demand for water and energy.
More people, housing and industries need more water and power.
Water scarcity is always caused only by low rainfall.
It is often due to over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access.

quiz.q: Fresh water is continually renewed by:
quiz.explain: The hydrological (water) cycle of evaporation, condensation and precipitation keeps renewing fresh water.
steps: Fresh water keeps getting renewed through evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
That is the hydrological (water) cycle.
Answer: The hydrological cycle
quiz.mistake: Thinks people create fresh water by pumping or dams

quiz.q: Which is the most common reason for water scarcity in India, according to your textbook?
options: Over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water
quiz.explain: Scarcity is mostly caused by over-use and unequal access, not only by low rainfall.
steps: The textbook says scarcity is not caused by low rainfall alone.
It is mostly caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access among social groups.
Answer: Over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water
quiz.mistake: Believes scarcity is only a natural problem

quiz.q: How does growing food production for a large population add to water scarcity?
options: More land is irrigated, including in the dry season
quiz.explain: Feeding more people needs more irrigated land and dry-season crops, which use large amounts of water.
steps: More people need more food.
So more land is irrigated, even in the dry season, which uses a lot of water.
Answer: More land is irrigated, including in the dry season
quiz.mistake: Does not connect irrigation with water demand

quiz.q: Pumping out too much groundwater through tube wells leads to:
quiz.explain: Pumping faster than rain can recharge the ground lowers the water table.
steps: Heavy pumping takes water out faster than rain can recharge the ground.
So the water table goes down.
Answer: A falling water table
quiz.mistake: Thinks groundwater is unlimited

quiz.q: A river flows through a town, but its water is full of factory waste and sewage. This is an example of scarcity caused by:
quiz.explain: Even when water is available, pollution makes it unfit to use, causing scarcity.
steps: Water is present in the river, but it is full of waste and sewage.
Water that is unfit to use causes scarcity because of poor quality.
Answer: Poor water quality
quiz.mistake: Thinks scarcity is only about the quantity of water

quiz.q: Sringaverapura, near Prayagraj, had a water harvesting system in the 1st century BCE that channelled the floodwater of which river?
quiz.explain: Sringaverapura near Prayagraj channelled the floodwater of the Ganga.
steps: Sringaverapura near Prayagraj had a 1st-century-BCE system for floodwater.
Prayagraj is on the Ganga, and it channelled the Ganga's floodwater.
Answer: Ganga
quiz.mistake: Does not connect Prayagraj with the Ganga

quiz.q: Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built in which century?
quiz.explain: Bhopal Lake was built in the 11th century.
steps: Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built in the 11th century.
Answer: 11th century
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the dates of ancient hydraulic structures

quiz.q: How do industries add to the demand for water?
options: They use no water at all
They use water in production and need power, much of which comes from hydroelectricity
quiz.explain: Industries are heavy users of water and also need energy, a large part of which comes from hydroelectric power.
steps: Industries use water in production.
They also need power, much of which comes from hydroelectricity.
Answer: They use water in production and need power, much of which comes from hydroelectricity
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link between industry, power and water

teach.ask: Gappu says: 'Rain falls every year, so how can there be water shortage?' Explain the causes of water scarcity.
teach.praise: Chirp! It's not only less rain — overuse, pollution and unequal sharing cause water scarcity!
teach.nudge: Good try! What happens when water is polluted or over-pumped? Does rain alone decide scarcity?

revise.summary: Fresh water is renewed by the hydrological cycle, yet many regions face scarcity. Scarcity comes mainly from over-exploitation, excessive use, unequal access and pollution — not just low rainfall.
focus: Causes of water scarcity — population, irrigation, industry, urbanisation, pollution
Why scarcity can exist even where water is plentiful
Effect of over-pumping on the water table
remember: Fresh water is renewed by the hydrological (water) cycle
Scarcity = over-exploitation + excessive use + unequal access among social groups
Over-pumping groundwater lowers the water table
Polluted water (domestic and industrial waste, chemicals, fertilisers) also causes scarcity
traps: Don't say scarcity is caused only by low rainfall.
Plenty of water is not the same as usable water — pollution can still cause scarcity.

learn.hook: One dam, many jobs: it can water fields, light homes, stop floods and even grow fish!
points: A dam is a barrier across flowing water that blocks or slows the flow, often creating a reservoir. Multipurpose projects use it for irrigation, electricity, water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding.
Jawaharlal Nehru proudly called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would link agriculture with industrial growth.
Examples: Bhakra Nangal (Sutlej-Beas basin) is used for hydel power and irrigation; Hirakud on the Mahanadi combines water conservation with flood control.

Problems: dams disrupt a river's natural flow, cause sedimentation in reservoirs, affect aquatic life and fish migration, submerge forests and soil, and displace local communities. Over-irrigation can cause salinisation of soil, and sharing of water can lead to inter-state disputes.
Movements such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan (about the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada) and the Tehri Dam Andolan raised concerns about displaced people and the environment.

example.q: A dam was built to control floods, yet the area downstream flooded badly after very heavy rain. How can this happen?
steps: Over the years, sediment settles in the reservoir and reduces how much water it can hold.
During extreme rain the reservoir fills quickly, and water must be released.
Large releases from the dam can flood the area downstream.
example.answer: Sedimentation reduces storage, and excess water released during heavy rain can cause floods.

learn.reallife: The electricity that runs the fans in many homes of Punjab and Himachal Pradesh comes partly from hydel projects like Bhakra Nangal.

quiz.q: Who called dams the 'temples of modern India'?
quiz.explain: Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would help both farming and industry grow.
steps: Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India'.
He believed they would link agriculture with industrial growth.
Answer: Jawaharlal Nehru
quiz.mistake: Guesses another national leader

quiz.q: The Bhakra Nangal project is in which river basin?
quiz.explain: Bhakra Nangal is in the Sutlej-Beas basin and is used for hydel power and irrigation.
steps: Bhakra Nangal is in the Sutlej-Beas basin.
It is used for hydel power and irrigation.
Answer: Sutlej-Beas
quiz.mistake: Confuses Bhakra Nangal with Hirakud (Mahanadi)

quiz.q: The Hirakud project is on which river?
quiz.explain: Hirakud is on the Mahanadi in Odisha; it combines water conservation with flood control.
steps: Hirakud is on the Mahanadi.
It combines water conservation with flood control.
Answer: Mahanadi

quiz.q: Why are they called 'multipurpose' river projects?
options: They are built on many rivers at once
They are built by many countries
One project serves many uses such as irrigation, power, flood control and water supply
quiz.explain: A single project serves several purposes at the same time.
steps: 'Multipurpose' means one project serves many purposes.
Irrigation, electricity, water supply, flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding.
Answer: One project serves many uses such as irrigation, power, flood control and water supply
quiz.mistake: Takes 'multipurpose' literally as many rivers or gates

quiz.q: The Narmada Bachao Andolan raised concerns about which dam?
quiz.explain: The Narmada Bachao Andolan focused on the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada, especially the rehabilitation of displaced people and the environment.
steps: The Narmada Bachao Andolan is about the dam on the Narmada.
That dam is the Sardar Sarovar Dam.
Answer: Sardar Sarovar Dam
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Tehri Dam Andolan

quiz.q: How does a big dam affect fish in a river?
options: It always increases the number of fish species
It blocks fish migration and changes their habitat
It has no effect on aquatic life
It makes the water saltier for sea fish
quiz.explain: Dams break the river's natural flow, so fish cannot migrate freely and their habitat changes.
steps: Dams disrupt the river's natural flow.
This affects aquatic life and blocks fish migration.
Answer: It blocks fish migration and changes their habitat
quiz.mistake: Assumes dams are only beneficial for fish because of fish breeding

quiz.q: Why does a reservoir slowly lose its storage capacity?
options: Sediment settles at the bottom of the reservoir
quiz.explain: Rivers carry sediment, which settles in the still water of the reservoir and fills it up over time.
steps: Rivers carry sediment, which settles in the still water behind a dam.
Sedimentation fills the reservoir and reduces storage.
Answer: Sediment settles at the bottom of the reservoir
quiz.mistake: Does not understand sedimentation

quiz.q: Over-irrigation from canals of big dams can lead to:
quiz.explain: Too much irrigation raises the water table and brings salts to the surface, making soil saline.
steps: Too much canal irrigation raises the water table and brings salts up.
This causes salinisation of the soil.
Answer: Salinisation of the soil
quiz.mistake: Thinks more water is always good for soil

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Dams give water and electricity, so why do some people protest against them?' Explain multipurpose projects and their problems.
teach.praise: Chirp! Dams bring water and power, but we must care for displaced people, rivers and fish too!
teach.nudge: Good! Now tell me some problems dams can cause — for people and for rivers.

revise.summary: Multipurpose river projects use one dam for irrigation, power, water supply, flood control, navigation and more; Nehru called dams 'temples of modern India'. But dams also cause sedimentation, harm aquatic life, displace people and can lead to salinisation and disputes.
focus: Uses of multipurpose projects and examples (Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud)
Movements against dams — Narmada Bachao Andolan, Tehri Dam Andolan
remember: Nehru: dams are the 'temples of modern India'
Bhakra Nangal — Sutlej-Beas basin, hydel power + irrigation; Hirakud — Mahanadi, conservation + flood control
Problems: disrupted flow, sedimentation, harm to fish, submergence, displacement, salinisation, inter-state disputes
Narmada Bachao Andolan — Sardar Sarovar Dam
traps: Hirakud is on the Mahanadi, not the Narmada.
Don't think big dams bring only benefits — they also cause sedimentation, harm fish migration and displace people.

learn.hook: In the Thar desert, families once stored every drop of rain under their homes in tanks as big as rooms — and called it 'palar pani'!
points: Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rainwater for later use. Traditional Indian methods are cheap, eco-friendly and suited to local conditions.
In hilly regions of the western Himalayas, people built diversion channels called 'guls' or 'kuls' for farming. In the floodplains of Bengal, people built inundation channels to irrigate fields.
In arid and semi-arid Rajasthan, fields were turned into rain-fed storage structures, such as 'khadins' in Jaisalmer and 'johads' in other areas, to keep the soil moist.

In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer (Rajasthan), rooftop rainwater was piped into underground 'tankas'. The first spell of rain was not collected, to clean the roof and pipes. This stored water, called 'palar pani', was considered the purest form of natural water, and rooms built next to tankas stayed cool in summer.

Today: Tamil Nadu was the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses; Gendathur village in Karnataka harvests rooftop rainwater in about 200 households; Shillong in Meghalaya meets part of its household needs this way; and Meghalaya has a 200-year-old system of bamboo drip irrigation.

example.q: Why did families in Rajasthan let the first rain of the season flow away instead of storing it in the tanka?
steps: The first rain washes dust, leaves and bird droppings off the roof and pipes.
If that water entered the tanka, the stored drinking water would become dirty.
So the first spell was let go, and the cleaner rain that followed was stored.
example.answer: The first rain cleans the roof and pipes, so only the cleaner later rain is stored.

learn.reallife: Many apartment buildings in Chennai and Bengaluru now have rooftop pipes leading rain into recharge pits — a modern version of the old tanka idea.

games.title: Match the method to its region

items.text: Rainwater stored in tankas in Rajasthan was called ___.
___ was the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses.
Meghalaya has a 200-year-old system of ___ drip irrigation.
Gendathur, a village that harvests rooftop rainwater, is in ___.

quiz.q: 'Guls' or 'kuls' are diversion channels found in:
quiz.explain: In the hilly western Himalayas, people built guls or kuls to divert stream water for farming.
steps: Guls or kuls are diversion channels built in hilly areas.
They are found in the western Himalayas.
Answer: The western Himalayas
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the regions of traditional water systems

quiz.q: What were 'tankas' in Rajasthan?
options: Underground tanks for storing rooftop rainwater
quiz.explain: Tankas were underground tanks, often inside the house or courtyard, linked to the sloping roof by a pipe.
steps: In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, rooftop rain was piped into underground tanks.
These underground tanks are called tankas.
Answer: Underground tanks for storing rooftop rainwater
quiz.mistake: Confuses tankas with canals or dams

quiz.q: In Rajasthan, the rainwater stored in tankas was called 'palar pani'. Why was it valued so much?
options: It was salty and good for cooking
It was considered the purest form of natural water
It was used only for washing clothes
quiz.explain: Palar pani was considered the purest natural water and was relied on until the next rains.
steps: The water stored in tankas was called palar pani.
It was considered the purest form of natural water.
Answer: It was considered the purest form of natural water
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of palar pani

quiz.q: Which was the first Indian state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses?
quiz.explain: Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory for all houses, with penalties for defaulters.
steps: Tamil Nadu was the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses.
Answer: Tamil Nadu
quiz.mistake: Guesses a dry state like Rajasthan

quiz.q: Bamboo drip irrigation, about 200 years old, is practised in:
quiz.explain: In Meghalaya, bamboo pipes carry water from streams and springs downhill to plants, using gravity.
steps: Meghalaya has a 200-year-old system of bamboo drip irrigation.
Answer: Meghalaya
quiz.mistake: Mixes up traditional methods of different states

quiz.q: Inundation channels were developed in the floodplains of Bengal to:
options: Drain water into the sea quickly
quiz.explain: People built inundation channels to carry floodwater to irrigate fields.
steps: In the floodplains of Bengal, people built inundation channels.
They carried floodwater to irrigate fields.
Answer: Irrigate fields using floodwater
quiz.mistake: Thinks the channels were only for drainage or power

quiz.q: Khadins in Jaisalmer and johads in Rajasthan were used to:
options: Store rainwater in fields and moisten the soil for crops
quiz.explain: Agricultural fields were turned into rain-fed storage areas so that water stood and moistened the soil.
steps: In arid Rajasthan, fields were turned into rain-fed storage structures (khadins, johads).
The stored water kept the soil moist for crops.
Answer: Store rainwater in fields and moisten the soil for crops
quiz.mistake: Does not know the purpose of khadins and johads

quiz.q: Which of these is an advantage of rooftop rainwater harvesting in cities?
options: It recharges groundwater and reduces dependence on tankers
quiz.explain: Rooftop harvesting stores rain or sends it into the ground, raising groundwater and reducing shortages.
steps: Rooftop harvesting stores rain or sends it into the ground.
This recharges groundwater and reduces dependence on tankers.
Answer: It recharges groundwater and reduces dependence on tankers
quiz.mistake: Confuses benefits with harms

teach.ask: Gappu is curious: 'How did people in the desert get water without taps?' Explain rainwater harvesting with examples.
teach.praise: Chirp! Tankas, kuls, khadins and bamboo pipes — Indians have been saving rain for centuries!
teach.nudge: Nice! Can you name a traditional method, like tankas or kuls, and say how it stores water?

revise.summary: Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rainwater for later use. India has many traditional methods — guls/kuls, inundation channels, khadins, johads and tankas — and modern rooftop harvesting is spreading.
focus: Matching each traditional method to its region
Tankas and palar pani in Rajasthan
Modern examples — Tamil Nadu, Gendathur, Shillong, Meghalaya bamboo drip irrigation
remember: Guls/kuls — western Himalayas; inundation channels — Bengal floodplains
Khadins (Jaisalmer), johads — rain-fed storage in fields, Rajasthan
Tankas — underground tanks in Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer; stored water = palar pani, purest natural water
Tamil Nadu first to make rooftop harvesting compulsory; Meghalaya — 200-year-old bamboo drip irrigation
traps: Guls/kuls are in the western Himalayas, not Rajasthan.
The first spell of rain was not stored in tankas — it cleaned the roof and pipes.
